Cosmos-H-Surgical: Learning Surgical Robot
Policies from Videos via World Modeling

action–text alignment dataset comprising 2,447
expert-annotated video clips (over 300k frames)
collected across 8 different surgery types. Each clip
captures one of four fundamental actions: needle
grasping (689), needle puncture (989), suture pulling
(475), and knotting (294), which provides diverse
visualandproceduralcoverage. SATAiscuratedbyag-
gregating and re-annotating videos from credentialed
YouTube surgical channels [32] and publicly available
datasets, including GraSP [33], SAR-RARP50 [34],
Multiypass140 [35], SurgicalActions160 [36], Auto-
Laparo [37], and HeiCo [38].

We collected a total of 60 successful human-
teleoperated demonstrations for training and testing.
Each episode includes synchronized endoscopic video
(average length: 217 frames) and corresponding action
kinematics. In addition to these task-specific demon-
strations, we also utilized 66 out-of-domain episodes
(around 60k action frames pairs) depicting general
robot movements unrelated to the needle pickup task.
These data are used to pretrain a foundational inverse
dynamics model (IDM) for the surgical robot, provid-
ing transferable motion understanding across tasks.
The robot states are the same as the action
kinematics with the same dimension and values.

we evaluate
our method using the “Needle Pickup and Hand-Over”
task on rubber pad. The experiments are conducted
on a commercial endoscopic surgical system (robot
and manufacturer anonymized), which consists of a
stereo endoscope and two articulated robotic forceps
(left and right arms).

represents the translational
offset (cartesian coordinates) of the left forcep tip
with respect to the endoscope frame (represented
by meters).

radians.
The same definitions apply for the right forcep
withp 𝑅,r 𝑅, and𝑔𝑅. This yields a total of 20 control
dimensions. All translation and rotation components
are expressed relative to the endoscope’s coordinate
frame to ensure view-consistent control.

We adopt Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) [41] to effi-
cientlyspecializeCosmos-Predict2.5[ 1]forthesurgical
domain while preserving its general video modeling
capabilities. LoRAmodulesareinsertedintothetrans-
former’s attention and feed-forward layers, enabling
parameter-efficient finetuning with minimal forgetting.
During adaptation, the model learns to predict future
latent video frames conditioned on an initial observa-
tion and text prompt. Given an initial frame𝐼0, the
world model produces a rollout^𝐼1 :𝑇 =𝒲𝜃 (𝐼0), where
𝒲𝜃 denotes Cosmos-Predict2.5 [1] augmented with
LoRA adapters. A spatiotemporal encoder extracts
features from𝐼0, a transformer-based latent dynamics
module models temporal evolution, and a decoder re-
constructs the predicted frames.

These two
models predict robotic actions with DIT [44] and flow
matching heads [42]. The major difference is that
IDM’s inputs are two frames from the same video
(T = 16 frames apart), and the model predicts the
robot actions for every frame between these two input
frames, while the GR00T policy model takes the
current frame and text prompt, together with the
robot state to predict the actions for future 16 frames.

capability_assessments.rationale: Four settable procedural-text alternatives produce compared future scenes from the same origin. Functional qualitative L3 does not establish numerical-control dynamics or causal identification. Separate one-step fidelity and all lower-level tests are not inherited. A synthetic-assisted policy is implemented, but offline command imitation is insufficient here for demonstrated L4 decision/control capability. Horizon description: Qualitative same-origin multiframe alternatives; duration not_reported. No numerical horizon is reported for Figure5. The scope retains the exact model and matched-prompt evaluation; implementation descriptions of that same model are not different tested time regimes.

scope.endpoint: Offline command prediction from rubber-pad demonstrations
scope.boundary: Bench recordings, not learned-policy closed-loop execution or actual human clinical validation
Human video-reader assessment of the generator component only; not composed-policy effectiveness, autonomous care, patient validation or an independent replication.

gate_assessments.rationale: Source attribution and episode holdout are partial. Overlap, availability semantics and training-only preprocessing are insufficiently established.
Learned scene prediction exists; scope-matched successor-reference fidelity is not established by whole-video realism alone.
Generator maximum extent, cadence, drift curve, acceptance tolerance and effective horizon are unreported.
The adopted research interpretation asserts neither probabilistic guarantees nor uncertainty-dependent decisions. Calibration remains not_reported; risk-dependent use would make this gate applicable.
Semantic commands and matched alternatives exist; sufficient parameterization, timing and context-conditioned support remain unresolved.
No identified intervention-effect interpretation is adopted. Therapeutic or physically identified effect assurance would require a separate causal/mechanistic assessment.
An assisted policy is implemented, but sufficient decision/control endpoints and exploitation/mismatch tests are missing.
Hazard-matched guards, abstention, safe stop and escalation tests are unreported. Safe autonomy is not established.
Qualitative composition and adapted-transfer tests exist, but overlap controls and independent composition validation remain insufficient.
Actual ratings establish R4 existence; sampling, allocation, guidance, blinding and reliability remain insufficient for an assurance pass.
The demonstrated use is not live patient/workflow benefit evaluation. Prospective utility remains not_reported.

gate_assessments.rationale: No defined operational product/use/jurisdiction release is established. Research links do not authorize clinical use; asset access and governance remain unresolved.
